lesson.title: One, none or many solutions

lead.text: Each equation in two unknowns picks out a line of points on a sheet of graph paper. The equation x + y = 3 holds for (3, 0), (2, 1) and (0, 3), and for every point between and beyond them, all of which lie on one straight line. A solution of two equations is a point that lies on both lines.

Two straight lines can meet in three ways. They can cross at a single point, so there is exactly one solution: x + y = 3 and x − y = 1 cross at (2, 1). They can run side by side and never meet, so there is no solution: x + y = 3 and x + y = 5 cannot both hold, since x + y cannot be 3 and 5 together. Or they can lie on top of each other, so every point of the line is a solution: x + y = 2 and 3x + 3y = 6 are the same line, because dividing the second by 3 gives the first.
Every pair of equations falls into one of these three cases, and the numbers will tell us which.
Divide the second statement by 2 and compare it with the first.

reveal.text: Halving the second statement gives x + y = 4.5, a line that runs beside x + y = 4 and never meets it. No pair satisfies both.

lead.text: Row reduction shows the same cases in the numbers. Start with x₁ + 3x₂ = 2 and 2x₁ + 6x₂ = 7, and write the augmented matrix with rows (1, 3, 2) and (2, 6, 7). Subtract 2 times row 1 from row 2.

The second row becomes (0, 0, 3), because 2 − 2 × 1 = 0, 6 − 2 × 3 = 0 and 7 − 2 × 2 = 3. Read it as an equation: 0x₁ + 0x₂ = 3, which says 0 = 3. No values of the unknowns make that true, and every solution has to satisfy every row. So the system has no solution, which is the case of two lines that never meet.
A row like this is the signal to stop. Whatever the other rows say, no solution exists. The same reading holds for 0 = 5, or for 0 equal to any nonzero number.
Read the row as an equation and ask whether any values of the unknowns could satisfy it.

reveal.text: A row that reads zero equals a nonzero number cannot be satisfied, so there is no solution.

lead.text: Now change the right-hand side. Take x₁ + 2x₂ = 4 and 2x₁ + 4x₂ = 8. Subtracting 2 times row 1 from row 2 turns the second row into (0, 0, 0), because 8 − 2 × 4 = 0 as well. The row reads 0 = 0, which is always true and tells us nothing new. The second equation was a double of the first, so it added no information.

That leaves one real equation, x₁ + 2x₂ = 4, for two unknowns. Choose any value for x₂ and x₁ follows. Choose x₂ = 0 and x₁ = 4, or choose x₂ = 1 and x₁ = 2. Every such pair satisfies both original equations, and the choices never run out.

Here x₂ can be anything, so it is called a free variable. A system with at least one solution is called consistent, and a consistent system with a free variable has infinitely many solutions. This is the case of two lines lying on top of each other.

workedSteps.text: Subtract 2 × row 1 from row 2. The second row becomes all zeros.
The zero row says 0 = 0, which is always true. How many solutions does the system have?

lead.text: The third case is the one you met in the last lesson. After reduction, each unknown has a row that pins it down. Take rows (1, 0, 4) and (0, 1, 1). They read x₁ = 4 and x₂ = 1, so there is exactly one solution.

The first nonzero entry of a row in a reduced matrix is called its pivot, and here the pivots are the two 1s. An unknown whose column holds a pivot is pinned by its row. A column with no pivot has no row to pin it, and that unknown is free, as x₂ was in the last example.

afterFigure.text: To read any system, look at the reduced rows. A row reading 0 = a nonzero number means no solution. Otherwise, if every column has a pivot there is one solution, and if some column has none there are infinitely many.

lead.text: Here the equations name both unknowns outright: x₁ = 2 and x₂ = 3.

reveal.text: You saw that each unknown is fixed by its own equation. Nothing is left free and nothing contradicts, so there is exactly one solution.

workedSteps.text: No values of x₁ and x₂ can satisfy it. The system has no solution.

lead.text: Subtract 2 times row 1 from row 2, and read what the second row says.

reveal.text: You compared the two equations and found them in conflict. After reduction that conflict is a row reading 0 = a nonzero number.

lead.text: Free variables can be counted. A reduced system has some number of unknowns and some number of pivots, and each pivot pins one unknown. Whatever is left over is free, so a consistent system has (unknowns − pivots) free variables.

Take four unknowns with x₁ + x₂ + x₄ = 6 and x₃ + x₄ = 2. The pivots are in columns 1 and 3, so x₂ and x₄ are free: 4 − 2 = 2. Choose x₂ = s and x₄ = t, and the rest follow: x₃ = 2 − t and x₁ = 6 − s − t. Every choice of s and t gives a solution.
When there are no free variables, a consistent system has exactly one solution. Each free variable adds a direction in which you can move without breaking any equation.

One family of systems always has an answer. When every right-hand side is 0, the system is written A x = 0. Put x = 0 in and every row becomes a sum of products with zero, so every row gives 0. The zero vector solves every such system, and none of them can have no solution.

The question is whether there are others. Take x₁ − x₂ = 0 and x₂ − x₃ = 0, which have pivots in columns 1 and 2, so x₃ is free. Choose x₃ = t, and then x₂ = t and x₁ = t. Every solution has all three values equal: (0, 0, 0), (1, 1, 1), (2, 2, 2) and so on.
Three unknowns less two pivots leaves one free variable, so this system has infinitely many solutions. A system A x = 0 has either the zero vector alone as its solution or infinitely many.
A shop's three prices satisfy x₁ + x₃ = 3 and x₂ + 2x₃ = 4. The system is consistent.

lesson.orientation: Classify systems using contradictions, pivots and free variables.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: I'm thinking of two numbers, x and y. I tell you that x + y = 4, and then I tell you that 2x + 2y = 9. You can try to find them, but something is odd. The second statement looks like a double of the first, and doubling 4 does not give 9.

Until now every system had exactly one answer, and the row-reduction routine always ended with each unknown pinned down. Some systems end differently. Some have no answer at all, as this one seems to have, and some have so many answers that you can never list them all.
This lesson learns to read the last rows of a reduced system and say which case you are in. We start with a picture of two lines on a sheet of paper, and then see the same three cases in the numbers.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell from the reduced rows whether a system has one solution, none or infinitely many.

recap.keyIdea: After row reduction, a row reading 0 = a nonzero number means no solution. A consistent system with a free variable has infinitely many, and with none it has exactly one.

blocks.text: Back at the two statements about x and y, the second was a double of the first with the wrong right-hand side, so no pair satisfied both. You saw that two lines can cross, miss or coincide, and that free variables are the unknowns without a pivot.

recap.nextHook: The free variables of a system describe a shape, such as a line or a plane of solutions. The next lesson names that shape and asks which sets of vectors can be built from a few of them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Doubling the first gives 2x + 2y = 8, which contradicts 2x + 2y = 9. No pair works.

questions.prompt: I'm thinking of two numbers, x and y. I tell you that x + y = 4 and 2x + 2y = 9. How many pairs of numbers (x, y) satisfy both statements?
hints: How are the two left-hand sides related?
Double the first statement.
Compare what you get with the second statement.

misconceptions.feedback: Doubling the first statement gives a different right-hand side from the second. Check whether they agree.

questions.onCorrect: None. The two statements contradict each other. A reduced row reading 0 = a nonzero number signals exactly this.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The row says 0 = 5, which is never true, so the system has no solution.

questions.prompt: A row of a reduced system reads 0 = 5. How many solutions does the system have?
hints: Can any values of the unknowns make zero equal five?
A row is an equation that every solution must satisfy.
What does an impossible equation do to the whole system?

misconceptions.feedback: No values of the unknowns can make that row true, so no single answer can exist either.

questions.onCorrect: No solution. A row that reads zero equals a nonzero number cannot be satisfied.

questions.prompt: How many solutions do x₁ = 2 and x₂ = 3 have?
hints: Does either equation contradict the other, or leave an unknown free?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each unknown is fixed by its own equation: exactly one solution.

misconceptions.feedback: Both equations can be true at once: each one fixes a different unknown.
Each unknown is pinned down by its own equation, so nothing is left free.

questions.onCorrect: Each equation fixes one unknown, with no conflict and nothing free: exactly one solution.

acceptedIdeas: No values of the unknowns can make zero equal one.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every solution must satisfy every row, and no values make 0 = 1 true.

questions.prompt: Why does a row reading 0 = 1 mean there is no solution?

choices.label: No values of the unknowns can make zero equal one.
The unknowns must all be zero.
The system has more unknowns than equations.

hints: Every solution must satisfy every row.

misconceptions.feedback: If all the unknowns were zero, the row would still read 0 = 1. It is false whatever the values.
That can happen with solutions too. This row fails for a different reason: it is simply false.

questions.onCorrect: Every solution must satisfy every row. No values make 0 = 1 true.

questions.prompt: How many solutions do x₁ + x₂ = 3 and 2x₁ + 2x₂ = 7 have?
hints: Subtract twice the first equation from the second. What does the remaining row say?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The reduced second row reads 0 = 1, which is impossible.

misconceptions.feedback: Two equations that are multiples of each other on the left cannot pin down two unknowns.
Check the right sides. The second would need to be double the first for the equations to agree.

questions.onCorrect: Reduce it and the second row reads 0 = 1: a contradiction.

questions.prompt: How many solutions do x₁ + x₂ = 3 and 2x₁ + 2x₂ = 6 have?
hints: Subtract twice the first equation from the second. What is left?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The second equation is double the first, so one unknown is free: infinitely many solutions.

misconceptions.feedback: The second equation is just double the first, so it adds no new restriction.
Check the right sides. They agree here: the second equation is exactly double the first.

questions.onCorrect: The second equation adds nothing, so one unknown stays free: infinitely many solutions.

questions.prompt: A consistent system has x₁ + x₃ = 3 and x₂ + 2x₃ = 4. How many free variables does it have?
hints: Count the unknowns, then count the pivot columns.
Free variables are the columns left without a pivot.
Subtract the number of pivots from the number of unknowns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are three variable columns and two pivots, leaving one free variable.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of pivots. Free variables are the columns left over.
That counts all the unknowns. Only columns without a pivot are free.

questions.onCorrect: Unknowns minus pivots: three variable columns less two pivots leaves one free variable.

questions.prompt: Does every system A x = 0 include the zero vector as a solution?
hints: Put x = 0 into A x and see what comes out.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. A times the zero vector is always the zero vector.

misconceptions.feedback: Try x = 0. Every entry of A x is a sum of products with zero, so the result is zero.

questions.onCorrect: A times the zero vector is always zero, so x = 0 solves every system A x = 0.

questions.prompt: How many free variables remain in x₁ + 2x₂ + 3x₃ = 0?
hints: How many unknowns, and how many equations?
One equation can fix only one unknown.
Subtract the number of pivots from the number of unknowns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One independent equation restricts three variables, leaving two free variables.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the equations. Free variables are the unknowns left over.
That counts all the unknowns. One of them is fixed by the equation.

questions.onCorrect: Three unknowns, one pivot: two free variables, each able to take any value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 unknowns less 2 pivots leaves 3 free variables.

questions.prompt: A consistent system has 5 unknowns, and its reduced form has 2 pivots. How many free variables does it have?
hints: Free variables are the unknowns without a pivot.
Count the unknowns, then take away the pivots.
Subtract the number of pivots from the number of unknowns.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of pivots. Free variables are the unknowns left over.

questions.onCorrect: Unknowns minus pivots: 5 − 2 leaves 3 free variables.
